full_title: 4.4 Quiz: Sketching with Slope m and a Point

questions.prompt: A line has slope \(m = \dfrac{3}{4}\) and passes through \((-2, 1)\). Starting at \((-2, 1)\) and using rise and run, which point is ALSO on this line?

choices.feedback: Swapped rise and run! Adding \(3\) to \(x\) and \(4\) to \(y\) uses slope \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). For \(m = \dfrac{3}{4}\), add \(4\) to \(x\) (run) and \(3\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-2 + 4,\; 1 + 3) = (2, 4)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), start at \((-2, 1)\) and move up \(3\) (\(y = 1 + 3 = 4\)) and right \(4\) (\(x = -2 + 4 = 2\)), landing on \((2, 4)\)!
Careful with the sign! Because \(m = +\dfrac{3}{4}\) is positive, moving right \(4\) means moving up \(3\) (not down \(3\)), giving \((-2 + 4,\; 1 + 3) = (2, 4)\).

Moving left \(4\) and up \(3\) has slope \(\dfrac{+3}{-4} = -\dfrac{3}{4}\). With positive slope \(+\dfrac{3}{4}\), step right \(4\) and up \(3\) to \((2, 4)\) (or left \(4\), down \(3\) to \((-6, -2)\)).

questions.prompt: You need to graph a line with slope \(m = 3\) passing through \((5, 4)\) on a \([-6, 6]\) grid. Stepping up \(3\) and right \(1\) goes off the grid to \((6, 7)\), so you step in the opposite direction (down \(3\) and left \(1\)). What point do you plot?

choices.feedback: Rewrite \(m = 3 = \dfrac{3}{1} = \dfrac{-3}{-1}\). Moving down \(3\) and left \(1\) from \((5, 4)\) gives \((5 - 1,\; 4 - 3) = (4, 1)\), which fits comfortably inside the grid!
Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(3\) and down \(1\) gives slope \(\dfrac{-1}{-3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). For slope \(3 = \dfrac{-3}{-1}\), move left \(1\) and down \(3\) to \((4, 1)\).
Moving right \(1\) and down \(3\) gives slope \(-3\), not \(+3\)! To keep the slope positive, reverse BOTH directions: left \(1\) and down \(3\) gives \((4, 1)\).
Moving left \(1\) and up \(3\) gives slope \(-3\) AND still falls off the grid! Reverse BOTH directions (left \(1\), down \(3\)) to land at \((4, 1)\).

questions.prompt: The line below was sketched starting from \((-3, -1)\) and stepping to \((3, 3)\) as shown by the dashed triangle. What are the slope \(m\) and \(y\)-intercept \(b\) of this line?

choices.feedback: You spotted \(b = 1\) nicely, but you put run over rise! Always put rise over run: \(m = \dfrac{+4}{+6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\).
Great simplification \(\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)! Look closely at the \(y\)-axis, though: the line crosses at \((0, 1)\) above the origin (not \(-1\)), so \(b = 1\).

The dashed triangle gives \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\), and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis right at \((0, 1)\), so \(b = 1\) (equation \(y = \dfrac{2}{3}x + 1\)).
The line climbs upward from left to right (both rise \(+4\) and run \(+6\) are positive), so the slope is \(+\dfrac{2}{3}\), not negative.

questions.prompt: A line with slope \(m = -3\) passes through \((2, -1)\). If you step backward from \((2, -1)\) to reach the \(y\)-axis (left \(2\) units), what \(y\)-intercept do you land on?

choices.feedback: Careful! Moving left \(2\) and down \(6\) would be a positive slope (\(\dfrac{-6}{-2} = +3\)). Because \(m = -3 = \dfrac{+6}{-2}\), stepping left \(2\) means going up \(6\): \(-1 + 6 = 5\), giving \((0, 5)\).
Rewrite \(m = -3 = \dfrac{3}{-1} = \dfrac{6}{-2}\). Moving left \(2\) and up \(6\) from \((2, -1)\) reaches the \(y\)-axis at \((2 - 2,\; -1 + 6) = (0, 5)\)!
You only stepped up \(3\) (for \(1\) unit left), which lands at \((1, 2)\)! Stepping a second unit left (total left \(2\), up \(6\)) reaches the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 5)\).
Watch the sign! Moving up \(6\) from \(y = -1\) gives \(-1 + 6 = +5\), not \(-5\), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, 5)\).

questions.prompt: Maya was asked to graph the line with slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) passing through \((2, 3)\), and she drew the red line below. What exact mistake did Maya make?

choices.text: She used a positive slope (\(+\dfrac{1}{2}\)) instead of a negative slope (\(-\dfrac{1}{2}\)).
choices.feedback: Look at Maya's dashed triangle: she moved down \(1\) and right \(2\), so her slope really is \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\)! Look closely at the coordinates of her starting dot instead.

choices.text: She swapped rise and run, moving down \(2\) and right \(1\) instead of down \(1\) and right \(2\).
choices.feedback: Check the dashed triangle carefully: vertical move is \(-1\) and horizontal move is \(+2\), so her slope is correct! The error is where she placed her starting point.

choices.text: She swapped the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of the starting point, plotting \((3, 2)\) instead of \((2, 3)\).
choices.feedback: Maya got the slope right (down \(1\), right \(2\)), but she went \(3\) right and \(2\) up to \((3, 2)\) instead of \(2\) right and \(3\) up to \((2, 3)\). Starting at \((2, 3)\) would step to \((4, 2)\) and \((0, 4)\).

choices.text: She started at the \(y\)-intercept \((0, 3)\) instead of the point \((2, 3)\).
choices.feedback: Look at the starting dot — it is not on the \(y\)-axis! She plotted \((3, 2)\), reversing the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of \((2, 3)\).

questions.prompt: A line has slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3}\) and passes through \((-4, 3)\). Starting at \((-4, 3)\) and stepping by rise and run, which point is also on this line?

choices.feedback: You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(2\) and down \(3\) uses slope \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\). For \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{3}\), add \(3\) to \(x\) (run) and \(-2\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-4 + 3,\; 3 - 2) = (-1, 1)\).
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3}\) is negative, moving right \(3\) means going down \(2\) (not up \(2\)), giving \((-4 + 3,\; 3 - 2) = (-1, 1)\).

You added the rise (\(-2\)) to \(x\) and the run (\(+3\)) to \(y\)! Remember, run changes \(x\) and rise changes \(y\): for \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{3}\), step right \(3\) and down \(2\) from \((-4, 3)\) to \((-1, 1)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-2}{3}\), start at \((-4, 3)\), move down \(2\) (\(y = 3 - 2 = 1\)) and right \(3\) (\(x = -4 + 3 = -1\)) to land right on \((-1, 1)\)!

questions.prompt: You are sketching a line with slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3}\) through \((5, -1)\) on a \([-6, 6]\) grid. Stepping down \(2\) and right \(3\) lands at \((8, -3)\), which falls off the grid! Reverse both directions (up \(2\) and left \(3\)). What point do you plot?

choices.feedback: Rewrite the slope by reversing both signs: \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{3} = \dfrac{2}{-3}\). From \((5, -1)\), moving up \(2\) and left \(3\) lands at \((5 - 3,\; -1 + 2) = (2, 1)\), cleanly inside the grid!

You only reversed the vertical step! Moving right \(3\) and up \(2\) creates slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\), not \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\). To keep the same slope, reverse BOTH directions (left \(3\), up \(2\)) to land at \((2, 1)\).

You only reversed the horizontal step! Moving left \(3\) and down \(2\) gives slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\), not \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\). Reverse BOTH signs (up \(2\) and left \(3\)) to stay on the line at \((2, 1)\).

Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(2\) and up \(3\) gives slope \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\). For \(m = -\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{3} = \dfrac{2}{-3}\), change \(x\) by \(-3\) and \(y\) by \(+2\) to reach \((2, 1)\).

questions.prompt: The line below was sketched starting from \((-4, 4)\) and stepping to \((4, 0)\) as shown by the dashed triangle. What are the slope \(m\) and \(y\)-intercept \(b\) of this line?

choices.feedback: You spotted \(b = 2\) cleanly, but you put run over rise! Slope is always \(\dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-4}{+8} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), not \(-2\).

From the dashed triangle, \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-4}{+8} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis right at \((0, 2)\), so \(b = 2\) (equation \(y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + 2\)).
Your slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) is right, but check the \(y\)-axis carefully: the line crosses at \((0, 2)\) above the origin (not \(-2\)), so \(b = 2\).
Watch the direction of the line! From left to right it falls downward (rise \(= -4\), run \(= +8\)), so the slope is \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\), not \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

questions.prompt: A line with slope \(m = 2\) passes through \((3, 4)\). If you step backward from \((3, 4)\) to reach the \(y\)-axis (left \(3\) units), what \(y\)-intercept do you land on?

choices.feedback: Rewrite \(m = 2 = \dfrac{-2}{-1} = \dfrac{-6}{-3}\). Moving left \(3\) and down \(6\) from \((3, 4)\) hits the \(y\)-axis at \((3 - 3,\; 4 - 6) = (0, -2)\)!
Watch the sign of the vertical change! Moving left \(3\) and up \(6\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+6}{-3} = -2\), not \(2\). To keep \(m = 2\), go down \(6\): \(4 - 6 = -2\), giving \((0, -2)\).
You only moved down \(2\) (for just \(1\) unit horizontally), which lands at \((2, 2)\) — not on the \(y\)-axis yet! Taking all \(3\) steps (left \(3\), down \(6\)) reaches \((0, -2)\).
You used the run (\(1\)) as the vertical change instead of the rise (\(2\))! For \(m = 2\), moving left \(3\) changes \(y\) by \(-6\), landing at \((0, 4 - 6) = (0, -2)\).

questions.prompt: Emily was asked to graph the line with slope \(m = \dfrac{2}{3}\) passing through \((-2, 1)\), and drew the red line below. What exact mistake did Emily make?

choices.text: Swapped the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of the starting point, plotting \((1, -2)\) instead of \((-2, 1)\).
choices.feedback: Look at the starting dot: Emily plotted \((-2, 1)\) in the exact right spot! Check the direction of the line instead — Emily stepped down \(2\) instead of up \(2\).

choices.text: Swapped rise and run, stepping up \(3\) and right \(2\) (slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\)) instead of up \(2\) and right \(3\) (slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\)).
choices.feedback: Check the numbers on the triangle: Emily still used \(2\) vertically and \(3\) horizontally, not swapped! The error is the vertical sign: Emily went down \(2\) instead of up \(2\).

choices.text: Flipped the sign of the starting point's \(x\)-coordinate, plotting \((2, 1)\) instead of \((-2, 1)\).
choices.feedback: Emily's starting point \((-2, 1)\) is actually plotted correctly! The mistake is the slope's sign: the red line has slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\) instead of \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).

choices.text: Flipped the sign of the slope, graphing a negative slope (\(-\dfrac{2}{3}\)) instead of a positive slope (\(\dfrac{2}{3}\)).
choices.feedback: Good eye! Emily started at the right point \((-2, 1)\), but moved down \(2\) and right \(3\) (slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\)) instead of up \(2\) and right \(3\) (slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\)), which would reach \((1, 3)\).

questions.prompt: You are sketching the line with slope \(m = \dfrac{2}{5}\) passing through \((-3, -2)\) on a \([-6, 6]\) grid. Starting at \((-3, -2)\), take one forward rise-over-run step to the right. Where do you land?

choices.feedback: You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(2\) and up \(5\) uses slope \(\dfrac{5}{2}\). For \(m = \dfrac{2}{5}\), add \(5\) to \(x\) (run) and \(+2\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-3 + 5,\; -2 + 2) = (2, 0)\).
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = \dfrac{2}{5}\) is positive, moving right \(5\) means going up \(2\) (not down \(2\)), giving \((-3 + 5,\; -2 + 2) = (2, 0)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{2}{5}\), start at \((-3, -2)\), move up \(2\) (\(y = -2 + 2 = 0\)) and right \(5\) (\(x = -3 + 5 = 2\)) to land right on \((2, 0)\)!

Moving left \(5\) and up \(2\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+2}{-5} = -\dfrac{2}{5}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = \dfrac{2}{5}\)! Step right \(5\) and up \(2\) from \((-3, -2)\) to land on \((2, 0)\).

questions.prompt: On a \([-6, 6]\) grid, a line passes through \((4, 3)\) with slope \(m = \dfrac{3}{4}\). Moving forward (right \(4\), up \(3\)) goes off the grid to \((8, 6)\). If you step backward instead (left \(4\), down \(3\)), which lattice point on the line do you reach?

choices.feedback: You only reversed the vertical step! Moving right \(4\) and down \(3\) creates slope \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). To keep the same slope, reverse BOTH directions (left \(4\), down \(3\)) to land at \((0, 0)\).
Rewrite the slope by reversing both signs: \(m = \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{-3}{-4}\). From \((4, 3)\), moving down \(3\) and left \(4\) lands at \((4 - 4,\; 3 - 3) = (0, 0)\), cleanly inside the grid!

You only reversed the horizontal step! Moving left \(4\) and up \(3\) gives slope \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). Reverse BOTH signs (down \(3\) and left \(4\)) to stay on the line at \((0, 0)\).
Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(3\) and down \(4\) gives slope \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). For \(m = \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{-3}{-4}\), change \(x\) by \(-4\) and \(y\) by \(-3\) to reach \((0, 0)\).

questions.prompt: The line below passes through \((-4, -4)\) and \((4, 2)\) with the dashed rise-and-run triangle shown. What is the equation of this line in slope-intercept form?

choices.feedback: From the dashed triangle, \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{+6}{+8} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis right at \((0, -1)\), so \(b = -1\) (equation \(y = \dfrac{3}{4}x - 1\)).
You spotted \(b = -1\) cleanly, but you put run over rise! Slope is always \(\dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{+6}{+8} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(\dfrac{4}{3}\).
Your slope \(m = \dfrac{3}{4}\) is right, but check the \(y\)-axis carefully: the line crosses at \((0, -1)\) below the origin (not \(1\)), so \(b = -1\).
Watch the direction of the line! From left to right it climbs upward (rise \(= +6\), run \(= +8\)), so the slope is \(\dfrac{3}{4}\), not \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\).

questions.prompt: Starting from \((4, 1)\) on a line with slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), walk left \(4\) units along the line until \(x = 0\). What is the \(y\)-intercept?

choices.feedback: Watch the sign of the vertical change! Moving left \(4\) and down \(2\) gives slope \(\dfrac{-2}{-4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), not \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\). To keep \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), go up \(2\): \(1 + 2 = 3\), giving \((0, 3)\).
You only moved up \(1\) (for just \(2\) units horizontally), which lands at \((2, 2)\) — not on the \(y\)-axis yet! Taking all \(2\) steps (left \(4\), up \(2\)) reaches \((0, 3)\).
Watch the sign at the end! Starting at \(y = 1\) and moving up \(2\) gives \(1 + 2 = 3\) (not \(-3\)), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, 3)\).
Rewrite \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{+1}{-2} = \dfrac{+2}{-4}\). Moving left \(4\) and up \(2\) from \((4, 1)\) hits the \(y\)-axis at \((4 - 4,\; 1 + 2) = (0, 3)\)!

questions.prompt: Look closely at Minji's red graph for the line with slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) through \((-2, 4)\). Which mistake explains why Minji's line is wrong?

choices.text: Swapped the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of the starting point, plotting \((4, -2)\) instead of \((-2, 4)\).

questions.prompt: To graph a line through \((-2, -4)\) with slope \(m = 3\), start at \((-2, -4)\) and move horizontally by the run and vertically by the rise. Which lattice point do you plot next?

choices.feedback: You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(3\) and up \(1\) uses slope \(\dfrac{1}{3}\). For \(m = 3 = \dfrac{3}{1}\), add \(1\) to \(x\) (run) and \(+3\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-2 + 1,\; -4 + 3) = (-1, -1)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{3}{1}\), start at \((-2, -4)\), move up \(3\) (\(y = -4 + 3 = -1\)) and right \(1\) (\(x = -2 + 1 = -1\)) to land right on \((-1, -1)\)!
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = 3\) is positive, moving right \(1\) means going up \(3\) (not down \(3\)), giving \((-2 + 1,\; -4 + 3) = (-1, -1)\).
Moving left \(1\) and up \(3\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+3}{-1} = -3\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = 3\)! Step right \(1\) and up \(3\) from \((-2, -4)\) to land on \((-1, -1)\).

Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(3\) and up \(1\) gives slope \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\). For \(m = -3 = \dfrac{-3}{1} = \dfrac{3}{-1}\), change \(x\) by \(-1\) and \(y\) by \(+3\) to reach \((1, -2)\).

questions.prompt: A line through \((-3, -1)\) has slope \(m = \dfrac{2}{3}\). Move right \(3\) units from \((-3, -1)\) along the line to reach the \(y\)-axis. What \(y\)-intercept \((0, b)\) do you land on?

questions.prompt: Using Method 3 (slope and a point), start at \((-5, 4)\) and apply slope \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\) once to the right. Which ordered pair lies on the line?

choices.feedback: With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-3}{4}\), start at \((-5, 4)\), move down \(3\) (\(y = 4 - 3 = 1\)) and right \(4\) (\(x = -5 + 4 = -1\)) to land right on \((-1, 1)\)!

You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(3\) and down \(4\) uses slope \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\). For \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{-3}{4}\), add \(4\) to \(x\) (run) and \(-3\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-5 + 4,\; 4 - 3) = (-1, 1)\).
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\) is negative, moving right \(4\) means going down \(3\) (not up \(3\)), giving \((-5 + 4,\; 4 - 3) = (-1, 1)\).

Moving left \(4\) and down \(3\) gives slope \(\dfrac{-3}{-4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\)! Step right \(4\) and down \(3\) from \((-5, 4)\) to land on \((-1, 1)\).

choices.feedback: Check the dashed triangle: Eunji moved up \(3\) and right \(2\), so the slope really is \(\dfrac{3}{2}\)! Look at the starting dot instead: Eunji plotted \((-3, -1)\) instead of \((-1, -3)\).

choices.text: Swapped rise and run, stepping up \(2\) and right \(3\) (slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\)) instead of up \(3\) and right \(2\) (slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\)).
choices.feedback: Check the rise and run in the triangle: vertical change is \(+3\) and horizontal change is \(+2\), so the slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) is right! The mistake is swapping \((-1, -3)\) to \((-3, -1)\).

choices.text: Swapped the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of the starting point, plotting \((-3, -1)\) instead of \((-1, -3)\).
choices.feedback: Spot on! Eunji got the slope right (up \(3\) and right \(2\), matching \(m = \dfrac{3}{2}\)), but plotted \((-3, -1)\) instead of \((-1, -3)\). Starting at \((-1, -3)\) steps to \((1, 0)\).

choices.text: Flipped the sign of the starting point's \(y\)-coordinate, plotting \((-1, 3)\) instead of \((-1, -3)\).
choices.feedback: Look closely at the red starting dot: it sits at \((-3, -1)\), not \((-1, 3)\). Eunji reversed the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of \((-1, -3)\).

questions.prompt: A line has slope \(m = \dfrac{5}{3}\) and passes through \((-4, -3)\). Starting at \((-4, -3)\) and stepping by rise and run, which point is also on this line?

choices.feedback: You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(5\) and up \(3\) uses slope \(\dfrac{3}{5}\). For \(m = \dfrac{5}{3}\), add \(3\) to \(x\) (run) and \(+5\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-4 + 3,\; -3 + 5) = (-1, 2)\).
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = \dfrac{5}{3}\) is positive, moving right \(3\) means going up \(5\) (not down \(5\)), giving \((-4 + 3,\; -3 + 5) = (-1, 2)\).

Moving left \(3\) and up \(5\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+5}{-3} = -\dfrac{5}{3}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = \dfrac{5}{3}\)! Step right \(3\) and up \(5\) from \((-4, -3)\) to land on \((-1, 2)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\), start at \((-4, -3)\), move up \(5\) (\(y = -3 + 5 = 2\)) and right \(3\) (\(x = -4 + 3 = -1\)) to land right on \((-1, 2)\)!

questions.prompt: To graph the line with slope \(m = \dfrac{4}{3}\) passing through \((4, 5)\) inside \([-6, 6] \times [-6, 6]\), notice that going up \(4\) and right \(3\) reaches \((7, 9)\) (off the grid). Rewrite the slope with both signs reversed and step backward from \((4, 5)\). Where do you land?

choices.feedback: Rewrite the slope by reversing both signs: \(m = \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{-4}{-3}\). From \((4, 5)\), moving down \(4\) and left \(3\) lands at \((4 - 3,\; 5 - 4) = (1, 1)\), cleanly inside the grid!

You only reversed the vertical step! Moving right \(3\) and down \(4\) creates slope \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\), not \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). To keep the same slope, reverse BOTH directions (left \(3\), down \(4\)) to land at \((1, 1)\).

You only reversed the horizontal step! Moving left \(3\) and up \(4\) gives slope \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\), not \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). Reverse BOTH signs (down \(4\) and left \(3\)) to stay on the line at \((1, 1)\).
Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(4\) and down \(3\) gives slope \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). For \(m = \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{-4}{-3}\), change \(x\) by \(-3\) and \(y\) by \(-4\) to reach \((1, 1)\).

From the dashed triangle, \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-4}{+10} = -\dfrac{2}{5}\), and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis right at \((0, 1)\), so \(b = 1\) (equation \(y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x + 1\)).
Your slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{5}\) is right, but check the \(y\)-axis carefully: the line crosses at \((0, 1)\) above the origin (not \(-1\)), so \(b = 1\).

questions.prompt: A line with slope \(m = \dfrac{3}{5}\) passes through \((-5, -4)\). If you step forward from \((-5, -4)\) to reach the \(y\)-axis (right \(5\) units), what \(y\)-intercept do you land on?

Watch the sign at the end! Starting at \(y = -4\) and moving up \(3\) gives \(-4 + 3 = -1\) (not \(1\)), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, -1)\).
You took one slope step too many! Moving right \(5\) from \(x = -5\) reaches \(x = 0\) after a vertical change of \(+3\), landing at \((0, -1)\).

Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = \dfrac{1}{5}\) is positive, moving right \(5\) means going up \(1\) (not down \(1\)), giving \((-1 + 5,\; -4 + 1) = (4, -3)\).

Moving left \(5\) and up \(1\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+1}{-5} = -\dfrac{1}{5}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = \dfrac{1}{5}\)! Step right \(5\) and up \(1\) from \((-1, -4)\) to land on \((4, -3)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{1}{5}\), start at \((-1, -4)\), move up \(1\) (\(y = -4 + 1 = -3\)) and right \(5\) (\(x = -1 + 5 = 4\)) to land right on \((4, -3)\)!

Watch the sign at the end! Starting at \(y = -5\) and moving up \(3\) gives \(-5 + 3 = -2\) (not \(2\)), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, -2)\).
You used the run (\(4\)) as the vertical change instead of the rise (\(3\))! For \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4}\), moving left \(4\) changes \(y\) by \(+3\), landing at \((0, -5 + 3) = (0, -2)\).
Rewrite \(m = -\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{+3}{-4}\). Moving left \(4\) and up \(3\) from \((4, -5)\) hits the \(y\)-axis at \((4 - 4,\; -5 + 3) = (0, -2)\)!

questions.prompt: A straight line passes through \((1, -5)\) and has slope \(m = \dfrac{3}{5}\). If you step right by the run and vertically by the rise from \((1, -5)\), which point do you reach?

choices.feedback: You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(3\) and up \(5\) uses slope \(\dfrac{5}{3}\). For \(m = \dfrac{3}{5}\), add \(5\) to \(x\) (run) and \(+3\) to \(y\) (rise): \((1 + 5,\; -5 + 3) = (6, -2)\).
With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), start at \((1, -5)\), move up \(3\) (\(y = -5 + 3 = -2\)) and right \(5\) (\(x = 1 + 5 = 6\)) to land right on \((6, -2)\)!
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = \dfrac{3}{5}\) is positive, moving right \(5\) means going up \(3\) (not down \(3\)), giving \((1 + 5,\; -5 + 3) = (6, -2)\).

Moving left \(5\) and up \(3\) gives slope \(\dfrac{+3}{-5} = -\dfrac{3}{5}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = \dfrac{3}{5}\)! Step right \(5\) and up \(3\) from \((1, -5)\) to land on \((6, -2)\).

questions.prompt: On a \([-6, 6]\) grid, a line passes through \((1, 5)\) with slope \(m = \dfrac{2}{3}\). Moving forward (right \(3\), up \(2\)) goes off the grid to \((4, 7)\). If you step backward instead (left \(3\), down \(2\)), which lattice point on the line do you reach?

choices.feedback: You only reversed the vertical step! Moving right \(3\) and down \(2\) creates slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\), not \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). To keep the same slope, reverse BOTH directions (left \(3\), down \(2\)) to land at \((-2, 3)\).

You only reversed the horizontal step! Moving left \(3\) and up \(2\) gives slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\), not \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). Reverse BOTH signs (down \(2\) and left \(3\)) to stay on the line at \((-2, 3)\).
Rewrite the slope by reversing both signs: \(m = \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{-3}\). From \((1, 5)\), moving down \(2\) and left \(3\) lands at \((1 - 3,\; 5 - 2) = (-2, 3)\), cleanly inside the grid!
Swapped rise and run! Moving left \(2\) and down \(3\) gives slope \(\dfrac{3}{2}\). For \(m = \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{-2}{-3}\), change \(x\) by \(-3\) and \(y\) by \(-2\) to reach \((-2, 3)\).

questions.prompt: Using the dashed slope triangle from \((-3, 0)\) to \((3, -2)\) and where the line crosses the \(y\)-axis, identify the slope \(m\) and \(y\)-intercept \(b\).

choices.feedback: You spotted \(b = -1\) cleanly, but you put run over rise! Slope is always \(\dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-2}{+6} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), not \(-3\).
Your slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) is right, but check the \(y\)-axis carefully: the line crosses at \((0, -1)\) below the origin (not \(1\)), so \(b = -1\).
Watch the direction of the line! From left to right it falls downward (rise \(= -2\), run \(= +6\)), so the slope is \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\), not \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).

From the dashed triangle, \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-2}{+6} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), and the line crosses the \(y\)-axis right at \((0, -1)\), so \(b = -1\) (equation \(y = -\dfrac{1}{3}x - 1\)).

questions.prompt: Starting from \((-2, -1)\) on a line with slope \(m = 3\), step right \(2\) units along the line until you hit \(x = 0\). What is the \(y\)-intercept?

choices.feedback: Watch the sign of the vertical change! Moving right \(2\) and down \(6\) gives slope \(\dfrac{-6}{+2} = -3\), not \(3\). To keep \(m = 3\), go up \(6\): \(-1 + 6 = 5\), giving \((0, 5)\).
You only moved up \(3\) (for just \(1\) unit horizontally), which lands at \((-1, 2)\) — not on the \(y\)-axis yet! Taking all \(2\) steps (right \(2\), up \(6\)) reaches \((0, 5)\).
Rewrite \(m = 3 = \dfrac{+3}{+1} = \dfrac{+6}{+2}\). Moving right \(2\) and up \(6\) from \((-2, -1)\) hits the \(y\)-axis at \((-2 + 2,\; -1 + 6) = (0, 5)\)!
Watch the sign at the end! Starting at \(y = -1\) and moving up \(6\) gives \(-1 + 6 = 5\) (not \(-5\)), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, 5)\).

questions.prompt: On a coordinate plane, plot \((-5, -2)\) and use slope \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) to step forward (to the right) to a second integer point. Which point is on this line?

choices.feedback: With \(m = \dfrac{\text{Rise}}{\text{Run}} = \dfrac{-1}{3}\), start at \((-5, -2)\), move down \(1\) (\(y = -2 - 1 = -3\)) and right \(3\) (\(x = -5 + 3 = -2\)) to land right on \((-2, -3)\)!

You swapped rise and run! Moving right \(1\) and down \(3\) uses slope \(-3\). For \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{-1}{3}\), add \(3\) to \(x\) (run) and \(-1\) to \(y\) (rise): \((-5 + 3,\; -2 - 1) = (-2, -3)\).
Watch the sign of the rise! Because \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) is negative, moving right \(3\) means going down \(1\) (not up \(1\)), giving \((-5 + 3,\; -2 - 1) = (-2, -3)\).

Moving left \(3\) and down \(1\) gives slope \(\dfrac{-1}{-3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), which is the opposite sign of \(m = -\dfrac{1}{3}\)! Step right \(3\) and down \(1\) from \((-5, -2)\) to land on \((-2, -3)\).
